Abstract
In December 2019, the first reported cases of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) emerged in Wuhan, China. In an attempt to control the spread of the disease, the Chinese government imposed a travel ban on Wuhan on 23 January 2020. In this paper, we use a simple mathematical model to study the effect of the travel ban on the spread of the disease in China. We show that the travel ban was crucial in reducing the number of cases in China. Without the travel ban, the number of cases in China would have been much higher than what was actually observed. We also show that the travel ban should have been imposed much earlier.

The curfew is in place to try to limit the spread of the coronavirus.

But with more than 1 million people living in Lusaka, and more than 600,000 in the Copperbelt, mass testing is the only way to find all the cases.

The problem is that mass testing is expensive and time-consuming.

The WHO recommends that countries test people who have symptoms of COVID-19, people who have been in contact with someone who has the virus, and people who work in the health sector.

This is known as targeted testing.

Targeted testing is more practical and cost-effective than mass testing, but it may not find all the cases.

This is because some people with COVID-19 may not have symptoms, or they may not know they have been in contact with someone who has the virus.

If these people are not tested, they may unknowingly spread the virus to others.

This is why some experts believe that mass testing is the only way to stop the spread of COVID-19.

Mass testing means testing everyone in a certain area, regardless of whether they have symptoms or not.

They found that the proportion of asymptomatic cases had to be high, and asymptomatic cases had to be less infectious, for the data to match the models. The only scenario with the right fit was 50% asymptomatic cases, who were half as infectious.

The researchers then used their winning model to look at how much COVID-19 cases and deaths would go up if social distancing measures were relaxed. They looked at 3 scenarios: no relaxation, mild relaxation (a 10% increase in social contacts), and strong relaxation (a 25% increase in social contacts).

They found that even mild relaxation led to a 2.8x increase in cases and a 3.5x increase in deaths, while strong relaxation led to a 6.7x increase in cases and a 7.8x increase in deaths. The only scenario that didn’t lead to explosive growth was no relaxation at all.

The researchers conclude that “a significant fraction of transmissions [of COVID-19] are occurring from individuals who never develop symptoms,” and that public health interventions need to account for this, for example by encouraging social distancing even when COVID-19 cases and deaths are still relatively low.

They also conclude that, “even modest relaxation of social distancing measures would be expected to result in explosive growth of COVID-19 cases and deaths.”

The researchers acknowledge that their study has some limitations. For example, they had to make some assumptions about the infectiousness of asymptomatic cases, and they only looked at data from Wuhan, so it’s not clear how well the model would apply to other places.

However, they note that “the model we have developed is freely available for others to use and further improve,” and that their findings are consistent with other recent studies that have suggested that asymptomatic transmission is important.

The study was published in the journal Science.

Evaluation of Visual and Cytology Screening in Preventing Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia
Evaluation of Visual and Cytology Screening in Preventing Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia
Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in women worldwide. In Namibia, cervical cancer is the most common cancer in women. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of visual screening (VS) and cytology screening (CS) in preventing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 and above (CIN2+) and cervical cancer. The study was conducted in the Ministry of Health and Social Services (MOHSS) screening program in Namibia. The study population consisted of 10,000 women aged 30-49 years who were screened for cervical cancer between 2010 and 2015. The screening program used both VS and CS. The results of the study showed that VS was more effective in preventing CIN2+ and cervical cancer than CS. The study also showed that the combination of VS and CS was more effective in preventing CIN2+ and cervical cancer than either VS or CS alone. The study concluded that VS should be used as the primary screening method for cervical cancer in Namibia. The study also recommended that CS should be used as a follow-up test for women who test positive for CIN2+ on VS. The study also recommended that the screening program should be expanded to include women aged 25-69 years.

Abstract 1016:
Sunday at 08:30 AM
Background: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is common in patients with HIV. The prevalence of HCV infection in hemodialysis patients with HIV is unknown.
Methods: We performed a cross-sectional study of all 149 patients who received chronic hemodialysis at our facility. The prevalence of HCV was determined by anti-HCV testing, followed by HCV RNA testing for a positive result. Demographic, clinical, and behavioral characteristics of patients with and without HCV were compared.
Results: The mean age of the study population was 50 years, 78% were male, and 92% were African American. Ninety-one (61%) were injection drug users. 39 (34%) were coinfected with HIV. HCV prevalence was 50% (95% confidence interval 44-56%). There was no significant difference in HIV coinfection (34% vs. 37%), duration of dialysis (5 vs. 5.8 years), history of incarceration (29% vs. 26%), or history of hepatitis A (14% vs. 10%) between HCV-positive and HCV-negative patients. There was a trend toward a higher prevalence of hepatitis C-related cirrhosis among HCV-positive patients (6% vs. 0%, p = 0.06). There was no significant difference in the frequency of other causes of cirrhosis (p = 0.6) or in the presence of encephalopathy (p = 0.6) between the two groups. Among injection drug users, the prevalence of HCV was 57% for those who had ever shared needles and 30% for those who had never shared needles (p < 0.01).
Conclusions: HCV infection is common in our hemodialysis population. Aggressive prevention efforts are needed to reduce the high prevalence of HCV infection in this population.

This means that both very low and very high levels of selenium intake were associated with an increased risk of disease, while moderate levels of selenium intake were associated with a decreased risk of disease. English:
The spatial and temporal dynamics of animal behavior are complex and diverse, with different species exhibiting unique patterns of activity and movement. For example, some animals are diurnal, meaning they are active during the day and rest at night, while others are nocturnal, meaning they are active at night and rest during the day. Some animals are crepuscular, meaning they are active during the twilight hours of dawn and dusk. Other animals are cathemeral, meaning they are active at irregular intervals throughout the day and night. In addition to these diurnal and nocturnal patterns, some animals exhibit seasonal patterns of activity and movement, such as migration or hibernation. These patterns are influenced by a variety of factors, including the availability of food and water, the presence of predators, and changes in temperature and daylight hours. Understanding the spatial and temporal dynamics of animal behavior is important for conservation efforts, as it can help identify critical habitats and migration routes that need to be protected. It is also important for managing human-wildlife conflicts, as it can help predict when and where animals are most likely to come into contact with humans. Overall, the study of animal behavior is a complex and fascinating field that continues to reveal new insights into the ways that animals interact with their environment and with each other.

A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Smartphone App for Improving Medication Adherence in HIV-Infected Adolescents in Botswana
Abstract
Background 
Poor adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) is common among HIV-infected adolescents and can lead to drug resistance and treatment failure. mSheduli, a smartphone app, has been developed to help adolescents improve adherence. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of mSheduli in improving ART adherence.

Methods 
This is a randomized controlled trial conducted in Botswana. Participants are 100 HIV-infected adolescents aged 13-21 years who are on ART. Participants are randomly assigned to either the intervention group, which receives access to the mSheduli app, or the control group, which receives standard care. The primary outcome is the change in ART adherence, measured by electronic medication event monitoring system (eMEMs) data, from baseline to 3 months. Secondary outcomes include viral load suppression, self-reported adherence, and quality of life.

Results 
The study is ongoing, and the results are not yet available.

Conclusion 
If mSheduli is found to be effective in improving ART adherence, it has the potential to be a valuable tool in the management of HIV-infected adolescents.

Trial Registration 
ClinicalTrials.gov NCT15334732.
Background
Adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) is critical for the effective management of HIV-infected adolescents. Poor adherence can lead to drug resistance, treatment failure, and increased morbidity and mortality. However, adherence can be challenging for adolescents due to various factors, including forgetfulness, stigma, and lack of social support. In this context, the development of innovative interventions to improve adherence is crucial. mSheduli, a smartphone app, has been developed to address these challenges and improve adherence among HIV-infected adolescents in Botswana.

mSheduli is a user-friendly app that provides reminders for medication intake, appointment scheduling, and symptom tracking. The app also includes features for peer support and counseling, which can help adolescents cope with the social and emotional challenges of living with HIV. The app is designed to be accessible and engaging, with customizable reminders and gamification elements that can motivate adolescents to adhere to their treatment regimen.

Biochar and compost improve soil quality for crops
Biochar and compost improve soil quality for crops
Published: 12 April 2017
A new study has found that adding biochar and compost to agricultural soils can improve soil quality and crop yields.
The research, published in the journal Geoderma, is the first long-term study to investigate the effects of biochar and compost on soil quality.
Biochar is produced by heating organic materials in low-oxygen conditions, while compost is made from the aerobic decomposition of organic materials.
The study, led by Dr. Daniel Murugesan from the University of Aberdeen, found that adding biochar and compost to agricultural soils can improve soil quality and crop yields.

The researchers produced corn cob, coconut and rice husk biochars using pyrolysis, which involved heating organic matter in the absence of oxygen, at 450 °C in a locally produced kiln.

The biochars were then used to treat 200 mL of water containing 100 mL each of 10 mg/L solutions of cadmium and lead, which are toxic heavy metals that often contaminate water in developing countries.

The team tested the biochars at loadings of 5, 10 and 15 grams per litre of solution. They found that after 90 minutes of contact time, the corn cob biochar removed 91% of the cadmium and the coconut shell biochar removed 96%. The rice husk biochar removed 94% of the lead, the corn cob biochar removed 86%, and the coconut shell biochar removed 92%.

The coconut shell biochar was the most effective at removing heavy metals from the water, the team reports in Chemosphere1.

The results suggest that the biochar could be used to treat water in developing countries, says study co-author and environmental chemist Siti Nur Aini Ibrahim at the University of Malaya in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. “The coconut shell biochar is the most effective, and it is available in Malaysia,” she says. “It could be used to treat water in rural areas.”

The biochars were also effective at removing fluoride, which can cause skeletal fluorosis, a painful bone disease, when it is present in high concentrations in drinking water.

The team is now working on scaling up the production of the biochars and testing them in the field, says Ibrahim. “We want to test them in the field, in water that is contaminated with heavy metals,” she says. “We want to see how effective they are in the field.”

Dr. Mercola

People with arthritis are at an increased risk of heart attack and stroke, even when their risk factors are optimally managed. In fact, a history of heart disease or stroke negates the benefits of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), the most effective medications used to treat inflammatory arthritis.

However, a new study published in the journal Arthritis Care & Research may have uncovered a possible explanation for this phenomenon. Researchers found that people with arthritis are more likely to have a blood clotting condition called hyperfibrinogenemia, which is associated with an increased risk of heart disease and stroke.

Hyperfibrinogenemia Could Explain Increased Risk of Heart Disease, Stroke in Arthritis Patients
Fibrinogen is a protein in your blood that helps form clots to stop bleeding when you are injured. However, if you have too much fibrinogen in your blood, it can lead to dangerous blood clots that can cause a heart attack or stroke.

In fact, elevated fibrinogen has been linked to an increased risk of all-cause mortality, coronary artery disease, heart attack, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease. Fibrinogen appears to promote atherosclerosis, the condition underlying all cardiovascular disease, by enhancing the retention of LDL cholesterol in the artery wall, where it becomes oxidized and triggers the inflammatory process that leads to atherosclberg plaque formation.

Studies have shown that people with inflammatory arthritis tend to have higher levels of fibrinogen than the general population, leading researchers to investigate whether hyperfibrinogenemia may play a role in cardiovascular disease in this population.

To find out, they reviewed data from 2,000 participants, average age 69, in the Osteoarthritis Initiative and the Tucson Epidemiological Arthritis Studies who did not have inflammatory arthritis at the start of the study. Forecast Product Co-Development and Scientific Accuracy/Consistency

The co-development of forecast products with stakeholders is a crucial component of the forecast value chain. It is the process by which the needs and requirements of stakeholders are integrated into the development of forecast products, ensuring that they are relevant, useful, and actionable. This process involves a range of activities, including stakeholder engagement, requirements gathering, product design, and testing and evaluation.

Document Type: book

Language: English
Description: Climate change is one of the defining challenges of our time. The food and agriculture sector is both vulnerable to and responsible for greenhouse gas emissions. In response, the UNFCCC has encouraged the identification and scaling up of climate-smart agriculture (CSA) interventions. However, the approaches used to assess the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions are not well established. This publication proposes a participatory approach to assessing the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions. It is based on a review of the relevant literature and a survey of 100+ practitioners. The proposed approach is intended to be used by practitioners to identify the strengths and weaknesses of an agricultural intervention in light of its effects on climate change mitigation, adaptation, and resilience. The approach is also intended to support the design of a monitoring and evaluation plan. The proposed approach is not intended to be a substitute for environmental and social impact assessments. It is also not intended to be a comprehensive assessment of an agricultural intervention. Rather, it is intended to be a rapid, participatory assessment of the climate-smartness of an agricultural intervention. Text:
Climate-Smart Interventions: A Concept Note
Climate-Smart Interventions: A Concept Note
Climate-Smart Interventions: A Concept Note
1. Introduction
The concept of climate-smart interventions is relatively new and has been developed in response to the need for more effective and sustainable approaches to addressing the impacts of climate change. The idea is to design and implement interventions that not only mitigate the effects of climate change but also enhance the resilience of communities and ecosystems to its impacts. However, there is a lack of clear and workable criteria as well as methods for assessing the climate-smartness of interventions. This concept note aims to provide a framework for evaluating the climate-smartness of interventions and to identify key considerations for designing and implementing climate-smart interventions.
2. Criteria for Assessing Climate-Smartness
There are several criteria that can be used to assess the climate-smartness of interventions. These include:
Mitigation: The extent to which the intervention reduces greenhouse gas emissions or enhances carbon sequestration.
Adaptation: The extent to which the intervention enhances the resilience of communities and ecosystems to the impacts of climate change.
Sustainability: The extent to which the intervention is environmentally, socially, and economically sustainable.
Equity: The extent to which the intervention promotes social equity and reduces inequality.
Participation: The extent to which the intervention involves and empowers local communities in its design and implementation.
3. Methods for Assessing Climate-Smartness
There are several methods that can be used to assess the climate-smartness of interventions. These include:
Life cycle assessment: This method assesses the environmental impacts of an intervention throughout its entire life cycle, from raw material extraction to disposal.
Cost-benefit analysis: This method assesses the economic feasibility of an intervention by comparing its costs and benefits.
Social impact assessment: This method assesses the social impacts of an intervention, including its effects on local communities and their livelihoods.
4. Key Considerations for Designing and Implementing Climate-Smart Interventions
There are several key considerations that should be taken into account when designing and implementing climate-smart interventions. These include:
Context: The intervention should be tailored to the specific context in which it will be implemented, taking into account local conditions, resources, and needs.
Participation: Local communities should be involved in the design and implementation of the intervention

The term “climate-smart agriculture” is something the United Nations encourages to help small-scale farmers prepare for climate change. It’s a concept that’s been around for a decade, but it’s only recently that the UN has been trying to make it a reality.
The idea is to help farmers adapt to climate change by using farming methods that are more resilient to extreme weather events, such as droughts and floods. It also involves finding ways to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture, which is one of the biggest contributors to climate change.
The UN has been promoting climate-smart agriculture as a way to help farmers increase their productivity while also reducing their impact on the environment. The hope is that by doing so, farmers will be able to feed a growing population without further damaging the planet.
But some critics say that climate-smart agriculture is just a way for big agribusinesses to continue profiting from the backs of small-scale farmers. They say that the UN’s approach is too focused on increasing productivity and not enough on addressing the root causes of climate change.
Others say that climate-smart agriculture is a good idea in theory, but that it’s not always practical for small-scale farmers. They say that many of the recommended farming methods require expensive equipment and technology that small farmers simply can’t afford.
Despite the criticisms, the UN continues to promote climate-smart agriculture as a way to help farmers adapt to climate change and increase their productivity. And with the global population expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, there’s a growing need for innovative solutions to ensure that we can feed everyone without further damaging the planet.
So, what does climate-smart agriculture actually mean? At its core, it’s about finding ways to make agriculture more sustainable in the face of climate change. This includes using farming methods that are more resilient to extreme weather events, reducing greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture, and finding ways to increase productivity without further damaging the environment.
It also involves working with farmers to help them adapt to changing climate conditions. This might involve providing training on new farming techniques, helping farmers access new markets for their products, or finding ways to help farmers cope with the economic impacts of climate change.
Ultimately, climate-smart agriculture is about finding a balance between the need to feed a growing population and the need to protect the planet. It’s a complex challenge, but one that we must address if we want to ensure a sustainable future for generations to come.

What scientists know about microscopic invaders that cause disease in South Africa
What scientists know about microscopic invaders that cause disease in South Africa
  • 11 min. to read
  • Published: February 10, 2023
  • Updated: February 13, 2023

This article is part of The Microscope, a new series that takes a microscopic look at what’s happening in a specific country. In this installment, we’re looking at South Africa.

In 1994, the election of Nelson Mandela as president ended apartheid in South Africa and ushered in a new era of democracy. The country has since held several peaceful elections, and its economy has grown steadily. But despite these positive developments, South Africa still faces many challenges, including high rates of crime, poverty, and unemployment.

In addition to these social and economic issues, South Africa also has a high burden of disease. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), South Africa has one of the highest rates of HIV/AIDS in the world. The country also has high rates of tuberculosis (TB) and malaria. These diseases are caused by microscopic invaders, or pathogens, that can be difficult to detect and treat.

In this article, we’ll take a closer look at some of the pathogens that cause disease in South Africa. We’ll also discuss the challenges of diagnosing and treating these infections, as well as the latest research on these microscopic invaders.

Apartheid assistant

One of the most well-known pathogens in South Africa is the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. TB is an ancient disease that has been around for thousands of years. It is caused by a bacterium called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This bacterium is spread through the air when people with TB cough, sneeze, or speak. TB primarily affects the lungs, but it can also affect other parts of the body, such as the brain, kidneys, and spine.

The economic impact of these outbreaks has been felt throughout the country, as the livestock industry is a significant contributor to the country’s GDP. The impact of these diseases on human health has also been significant, with many people falling ill and even dying as a result of these diseases. English: The study was conducted in the Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, University of Maiduguri, Borno State, Nigeria. The research work was carried out in the laboratory of the Department of Chemistry, Federal University of Technology, Akure, Ondo State, Nigeria. The study was conducted in the month of July 2021. The research work was carried out on 100 subjects, 50 male and 50 female. The age range of the subjects was 15 to 25 years. The consent of the subjects was obtained before the commencement of the research work. The blood samples were collected from the subjects in the morning before breakfast. The blood samples were collected in EDTA bottles. The blood samples were centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 minutes. The serum was separated and stored in a refrigerator at 4°C. The serum was used for the estimation of serum cholesterol, triglyceride, HDL, LDL, and VLDL. The kits were used for the estimation of serum cholesterol, triglyceride, HDL, LDL, and VLDL. The kits were used according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The data obtained were analyzed using SPSS version 20.0. The data were presented as mean ± standard deviation. The significance of the data was analyzed using one-way ANOVA. The p-value was considered significant at p < 0.05.

Cardiac arrhythmias are a common finding in patients with COVID-19. We aimed to assess the prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias in COVID-19 patients.

Methods: A literature search was conducted using PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library databases. Studies were included if they were original articles reporting the prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias in COVID-19 patients.

Results: Ten studies with a total of 1065 patients were included. The overall prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias was 12.3% (95% CI: 9.6–15.7%). The most common arrhythmia was supraventricular tachycardia with a prevalence of 3.7% (95% CI: 2.3–5.9%). Atrial fibrillation was the second most common arrhythmia with a prevalence of 2.1% (95% CI: 1.2–3.8%). Ventricular arrhythmias were present in 1.6% of patients (95% CI: 0.7–3.2%). Bradycardia was present in 1.4% of patients (95% CI: 0.6–2.9%).

Many Covid-19 patients had irregular heartbeats

Many patients with Covid-19 had abnormal heart rhythms, or arrhythmias, for up to three months after their initial infection, a new study finds.

The study, published in the journal JAMA Cardiology, is the largest to date to examine heart rhythm abnormalities in people who have had Covid-19.

The abnormalities were detected using a small device that continuously monitors heart rhythm and transmits the data to a smartphone app, which the patients used for 62 days after their initial infection.

The findings suggest that heart rhythm monitoring with the device could be a useful tool for identifying people who have had Covid-19 and might be at risk of developing heart problems, the researchers said.

“Covid-19 is a disease that affects multiple organ systems, and the heart is one of them,” said Dr. Ryan Gestring, a cardiologist at the University of Michigan and lead author of the study. “We know that Covid-19 can cause heart damage, but it’s not clear how common it is or how severe it might be in some patients.”

The new study suggests that heart rhythm monitoring with the device could be a useful tool for identifying people who have had Covid-19 and might be at risk of developing heart problems.

To conduct the study, the researchers recruited 1,000 people in Michigan who had tested positive for Covid-19 and 500 who had not. The average age of the participants was 51, and about half were women.

The researchers asked the participants to use the heart rhythm monitoring device for 62 days after their initial infection or after their last known exposure to someone with Covid-19. The device, which is worn like a patch on the chest, continuously monitors heart rhythm and transmits the data to a smartphone app.

The researchers found that 38% of the people who had Covid-19 had at least one abnormal heart rhythm, compared to 6% of the people who had not had the disease. Some of the arrhythmias were relatively benign, such as premature atrial contractions, which are an early heartbeat that originates in the atria, the upper chambers of the heart. Others were more serious, such as atrial fibrillation, in which the atria quiver rather than beat regularly

samples.src: Amblyomma hebraeum, the principal vector of Ehrlichia ruminantium in Southern Africa is widely distributed in the Southern District of Botswana and thus poses a challenge to livestock productivity in this district and, perhaps, elsewhere in the country where the tick infests livestock.
samples.ref: Amblyomma hebraeum, nga ke kawuka akasinga obukulu aka Ehrlichia ruminantium mu Southern Africa kasangibwa wangi mu Disitulikiti y’Obukiikaddyo bwa Botswana nga noolwekyo kaleetawo okusoomooza mu muwendo gw’ebisolo mu disitulikiti eno, era oboolyawo, n’awalala mu ggwanga enkwa gye ziruma ebisolo.
samples.hyp:
English:
The study area is located in the Southern District of Botswana, which is subdivided into 14 districts. The 14 districts are further subdivided into 77 sub-districts. The Southern District is located between 20° 45’ and 26° 24’ E and 20° 45’ and 30° 30’ S. The district has a total area of 262,480 km2 and a population of 443,482 (2001 census). The majority of the population (337,620) is involved in livestock keeping. The main livestock species are cattle (210,515), sheep (172,244) and goats (125,390). The climate is generally semi-arid to arid with mean annual rainfall ranging from 300 mm in the west to 600 mm in the east. The vegetation is mainly savannah with scattered trees and shrubs. High numbers of ticks in southern Botswana worsens heartwater disease in livestock
12 December 2019 at 11:01am
Ticks are a major problem for livestock in southern Botswana, and their numbers are increasing. This is making heartwater disease worse in the region.
Heartwater is a disease caused by the Coxiella burnetii bacteria, which is transmitted to animals by infected ticks. The disease is fatal in animals that do not have immunity, and causes high mortality rates in goats and sheep.
The disease is not a threat to human health, but it is a major problem for farmers in southern Botswana. The region is a major producer of livestock, and the disease is causing significant losses.
The increase in tick numbers is due to a number of factors, including climate change and land use changes. The disease is also being exacerbated by the movement of livestock between regions.
Farmers in the region are struggling to control the tick population, and are looking for new ways to manage the disease. Some are using acaricides, but these are not always effective, and can be expensive.
There is a need for more research into the disease and its control. This will help farmers to better manage the disease and reduce its impact on their livestock.
Source: Livestock Research for Rural Development

samples.hyp:
Read time: 1 minute, 32 seconds
A tick on a dog. (Shutter)
A study has found that domestic dogs in Uganda are hosts to disease-carrying ticks.
The study, published in the Parasites & Vectors journal, found that 42% of the 132 dogs it tested had ticks.
The research team, led by the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, removed and recorded the ticks, which were then tested to find out where they came from.
They collected 310 ticks between 2017 and 2019 from dogs in Arua (in the north of Uganda), Mbarara (in the south) and Fort Portal (in the west).
The ticks were found all year round, with the highest numbers recorded in the rainy season.
The research team found that the ticks collected from the dogs could transmit diseases to humans, including tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) and heartwater.
TBE is a viral infection that can cause flu-like symptoms and, in some cases, inflammation of the brain and spinal cord.
Heartwater is a tick-borne disease that affects mainly livestock, causing fever, breathing difficulties and death.
The study also found that some of the ticks were infected with TBE virus.
Uganda is an important migration route for ticks and the pathogens they carry.
The research team says that, while more research is needed, their findings suggest that there is a risk of people catching tick-borne diseases from dogs in Uganda.
They say that people should check their dogs for ticks, especially after they have been in areas where ticks are common.
The team also recommends that people take simple protective measures, such as wearing long sleeves and trousers, using insect repellent and checking themselves for ticks after being outdoors.

Barriers to Point of Care Testing in India and South Africa
English:
Barriers to Point of Care Testing in India and South Africa
The aim of this study was to understand the barriers to the adoption of Point of Care (POC) testing in India and South Africa. POC testing is defined as an analytical technique that can provide valuable clinical information at or close to the patient’s location. POC testing has the potential to improve patient outcomes by providing rapid results, improving access to healthcare, and reducing healthcare costs. However, the adoption of POC testing has been slow in India and South Africa, despite the potential benefits. This study aimed to identify the barriers to the adoption of POC testing in these two countries and to provide recommendations for overcoming these barriers.
The study used a mixed-methods approach, combining both qualitative and quantitative data collection methods. A total of 60 healthcare professionals from India and South Africa were interviewed, and a survey was also conducted among 200 healthcare professionals from these countries. The interviews and survey questions focused on the barriers to the adoption of POC testing, the perceived benefits of POC testing, and the factors that could facilitate the adoption of POC testing.
The results of the study identified several barriers to the adoption of POC testing in India and South Africa. One of the main barriers was the lack of awareness among healthcare professionals about POC testing. Many healthcare professionals were not familiar with POC testing and did not understand its potential benefits. Another barrier was the high cost of POC testing devices and reagents. POC testing devices and reagents were often more expensive than traditional laboratory testing methods, making them less accessible to healthcare providers in low-resource settings. The lack of regulatory approval for POC testing devices was also a barrier to their adoption. In both India and South Africa, the regulatory approval process for POC testing devices was slow and cumbersome, which discouraged healthcare providers from adopting these devices.
The study also identified several factors that could facilitate the adoption of POC testing in India and South Africa. One of the key factors was the need for increased awareness and education about POC testing among healthcare professionals. Training programs and educational materials could help healthcare professionals understand the benefits of POC testing and how to use POC testing devices effectively. Vol. 10 No. 1 (2022): Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
Articles
A genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies CENPJ as a host regulator of altered microtubule organization during Plasmodium liver infection
DOI:https://doi.org/10.3389/fcell.2022.837966
Keywords:
Plasmodium, liver stage, cell cycle, microtubules, CENPJ
Abstract
Plasmodium parasites undergo dramatic morphological changes during their development in liver cells. The parasites hijack the host cell machinery to build a parasitophorous vacuole, but also remodel the host cell cytoskeleton to form a unique shape. How the parasites alter the host cell microtubule network to achieve this is unknown. Here, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen to identify cellular host factors that regulate the microtubule network during liver stage infection. We identified 140 hits and performed follow-up analyses of several of them. We found that CENPJ, a component of the centriolar satellite complex, is relocated to the parasite-rimming microtubules during liver stage schizont formation. We show that CENPJ is specifically recruited to these microtubules in a parasite-secreted factor-dependent manner. CENPJ depletion leads to a disorganization of the liver stage schizont microtubule network and accumulation of tubulin at the parasitophorous vacuole membrane. Using live cell imaging, we show that centriolar satellites are dynamic structures that surround the parasites during liver stage development. Finally, we show that CENPJ depletion delays egress of merozoites from the liver stage schizont. Our results suggest that CENPJ and possibly other centriolar satellite complex components contribute to microtubule organization during liver stage infection to enable efficient egress of merozoites from the liver stage schizont.

Researchers must map combined effects of invasive species, climate change and human activities in South Africa
12.05.2021 - Source: University of Cape Town
Original article:
https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-021-01135-8
Climate change and invasive species are two of the biggest threats to biodiversity in South Africa. But the country’s biodiversity is also being affected by human activities, such as the overuse of water. To protect the country’s natural resources, researchers must map the combined effects of these factors, says Nadia Martin, an environmental scientist at the University of Cape Town in South Africa.
Martin is calling for a new national assessment of South Africa’s biodiversity, similar to the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services’s Global Assessment, which was published in 2019. That assessment involved more than 500 experts from around the world and found that more than 1 million species were at risk of extinction.
South Africa has not had a national biodiversity assessment since 2000, Martin says. In that year, the Convention on Biological Diversity — an international treaty — called for countries to assess their biodiversity every 10 years. South Africa’s most recent assessment, which was conducted in 2010, found that 10% of the country was protected, and that 34% of its species were threatened with extinction. But the assessment was not comprehensive, Martin says, and it did not include the country’s marine ecosystems.
Martin presented her case for a new assessment at a meeting of the South African National Biodiversity Institute in Cape Town on 28 April. She says that the new assessment should include a detailed analysis of the country’s protected areas, as well as the effects of climate change, invasive species and human activities on its ecosystems. It should also include an analysis of the country’s progress in meeting its commitments under the Convention on Biological Diversity, she says.
South Africa has set a target of protecting 10% of its land and oceans under effective management, in line with the Aichi Biodiversity Targets set by the Convention on Biological Diversity in 2010. English:
Biological invasions are a major driver of biodiversity loss worldwide, and South Africa is one of the countries that is highly affected by this phenomenon. The researchers wanted to know what kind of research is being done on this topic in South Africa, and how it is being done. They also wanted to know if there are any gaps in the research that need to be addressed.
The researchers used a method called bibliometric analysis to look at all the research articles that had been published on biological invasions in South Africa between 1990 and 2020. They looked at things like how many articles were published each year, which topics were most commonly studied, and which institutions and researchers were most active in the field.
They found that the number of research articles on biological invasions in South Africa has been increasing over time, with a total of 367 articles published between 1990 and 2020. The most common topics studied were the impacts of invasive species on native species and ecosystems, as well as the factors that contribute to the success of invasive species. The researchers who published the most articles were from universities in Cape Town, Pretoria, and Stellenbosch.
The researchers also found that there are some gaps in the research on biological invasions in South Africa. For example, there is relatively little research on the long-term impacts of invasive species, and on the effectiveness of different management strategies for controlling invasive species. They also noted that more research is needed on the interactions between invasive species and other global change drivers, such as climate change and land-use change.
Overall, this study provides a valuable overview of the current state of research on biological invasions in South Africa, and highlights areas where further research is needed. By addressing these gaps, researchers can help to better understand and manage the impacts of invasive species in this highly affected country.
Glossary:
biological invasions: when species like plants or animals are introduced into a new area where they thrive, become established and potentially harm other surrounding species or the environment.
biodiversity loss: the decrease in the variety of life on Earth, including the variety of species, ecosystems, and genetic material.
bibliometric analysis: a method used to analyze and quantify the production, dissemination, and impact of scientific literature.
management strategies: plans or actions taken to achieve a specific goal or outcome, in this case, controlling invasive species.
global change drivers: factors that are causing changes to the Earth's environment, such as climate change and land-use

How Ethiopia boosted chickpea production

Agriculture
11/01/2022 11:00

In Ethiopia, chickpeas are a staple food for millions of people, especially in the eastern and southern parts of the country.

The legume is also an important source of income for many smallholder farmers, who sell their crops to local markets.

However, Ethiopian chickpea production has been hampered by a number of factors, including low yields, pests and diseases, and a lack of access to improved seeds and other inputs.

To address these challenges, the Ethiopian government, in partnership with international organizations and local NGOs, has implemented a number of initiatives to boost chickpea production.

One of the most important of these initiatives has been the distribution of improved chickpea seeds to smallholder farmers.

These seeds are higher yielding and more resistant to pests and diseases than traditional varieties, and have helped to increase chickpea production in Ethiopia.

In addition to providing improved seeds, the government and its partners have also provided training and technical support to farmers on best practices for growing chickpeas.

This has included advice on crop rotation, soil management, and pest and disease control.

The government has also implemented a number of policies to support chickpea production, such as subsidies for inputs and price supports for farmers.

These policies have helped to make chickpea production more profitable for smallholder farmers, and have encouraged more farmers to grow the crop.

As a result of these efforts, chickpea production in Ethiopia has increased significantly in recent years.

According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Ethiopia’s chickpea production increased from 420,000 metric tons in 2015 to 600,000 metric tons in 2020.

English:
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Plant Science, found that the use of a platform that provided training and information on chickpea production increased the knowledge of farmers and led to an increase in production.
The study was conducted in India, where chickpeas are an important crop for many farmers. The platform used in the study was called "Chickpea Knowledge Management System" (CKMS), and it was designed to provide farmers with information on best practices for growing chickpeas, as well as training on how to use this information to increase their yields.
The study found that farmers who used the CKMS platform had a significantly higher level of knowledge about chickpea production than those who did not use the platform. They also had higher yields, with an average increase of 20% compared to the control group.
The authors of the study said that the CKMS platform was able to increase the knowledge of farmers because it was designed to be user-friendly and accessible. The platform was available in the local language, and it included videos and other multimedia resources that made it easy for farmers to learn about best practices for growing chickpeas.
The study also found that the use of the CKMS platform led to an increase in the adoption of best practices for growing chickpeas. Farmers who used the platform were more likely to use recommended planting dates, use recommended amounts of fertilizer, and use recommended pest control methods.
Overall, the study suggests that the use of a platform that provides training and information on chickpea production can be an effective way to increase the knowledge and yields of farmers in India and other countries where chickpeas are an important crop.

samples.hyp:
Reproductive Hormones Imbalance, Germ Cell Apoptosis, Abnormal Sperm Morphophenotypes and Ultrastructural Changes in Testis of African Giant Rats (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Exposed to Sodium Metavanadate Intoxication
1Department of Biology, Rivers State University, Port Harcourt, Nigeria
2Department of Biological Sciences, Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University, Bauchi, Nigeria
*Corresponding author: Olusegun O. Ogunlola, Department of Biology, Rivers State University, Port Harcourt, Nigeria
Submission: May 07, 2022; Published: May 19, 2022
ISSN 2637-4691 Volume 12 Issue 5

#### Abstract

The present study was designed to investigate the effects of Sodium metavanadate (NaVO3) on the reproductive hormones, testicular histology, sperm morphology, and ultrastructure of the testis of the African giant rats (Cricetomys gambianus). The animals were divided into two groups, the control and treated groups. The treated group was given 10mg/kg body weight of NaVO3 for 30 consecutive days. The results showed that NaVO3 significantly (P<0.05) reduced the serum levels of reproductive hormones (LH, FSH, and Testosterone) in the treated group. The histological analysis of the testis showed that NaVO3 caused germ cell apoptosis, abnormal sperm morphophenotypes, and ultrastructural changes in the seminiferous tubules of the treated animals. The occurrence of germ cell apoptosis and abnormal sperm morphophenotypes in the treated animals could be responsible for the reduced levels of reproductive hormones in the treated animals. The findings of the present study suggest that NaVO3 is a potential reproductive toxicant in C. gambianus.

#### Keywords: Sodium metavanadate; Reproductive hormones; Germ cell apoptosis; Sperm morphophenotypes; Ultrastructure; Cricetomys gambianus; Waterhouse; Seminiferous tubules

English text:
The study was conducted to evaluate the effect of sub-chronic exposure to sublethal dose of the pesticide, Sumithion (0.25 LD50) on the reproductive parameters of male Swiss albino mice. The parameters studied were sperm motility, mass activity, sperm abnormalities, histopathological changes in seminiferous tubules and immunohistochemical expression of P53 in seminiferous epithelium. The results showed that SMV treated group had statistically decreased sperm motility and mass activity with increased percentage of abnormal morphophenotypes of spermatozoa and upregulation of P53 immunopositive cell. The histopathological changes observed were vacuolization, shrinkage and degeneration of seminiferous epithelium, depletion of germinal cells and increased interstitial cell mass. The study concluded that sub-chronic exposure to sublethal dose of Sumithion had adverse effect on the reproductive parameters of male Swiss albino mice.

Homegardens are traditional agroforestry systems in the tropics and sub-tropics, which are characterized by a multistratified vegetation structure and a high degree of plant species diversity (Chhetri et al., 2006). They are open, managed, and structured landscapes, which are created and maintained by human intervention (Chhetri et al., 2006). Homegardens are a common feature in the traditional agricultural landscapes of the tropics and sub-tropics (Chhetri et al., 2006). They are a form of land use that has developed over a long period of time in response to the environmental and socio-economic conditions of the region (Chhetri et al., 2006). Homegardens are a rich source of food, fuel, fodder, and other non-timber forest products (NTFPs) (Chhetri et al., 2006). They are also a source of income for many rural households (Chhetri et al., 2006). Homegardens are an important component of the cultural landscape of many indigenous communities (Chhetri et al., 2006). They are an important source of cultural identity
